as $\varepsilon \to \infty$ it diffuses to the independence baseline
$P_{ij} = a_i b_j$, where improvement returns to zero. The grid from $0.1$
to $1000$ is wide enough that all three candidates peak in its interior on
each criterion, with the uninformative tails visible at each end. Binary
peaks in the interior too. As the one-parameter stay/move model described
in @sec-cost-metrics, its only lever is the aggregate stay/move split, so
its peak sits at the $\varepsilon$ where the diffusion of mass off the
diagonal matches the empirical move rate, and it peaks earlier than skill
and hierarchy, which keep improving as falling $\varepsilon$ sharpens an
off-diagonal allocation that pays off.
 
The two peaks rest on different footings. Peak $\Delta KL$ is a profile-likelihood model-selection criterion: because $\Delta KL$ is monotone in the maximised log-likelihood, maximising it over the grid profiles the likelihood over $\varepsilon$, the single unidentified scale parameter, so comparing peaks compares maximised likelihoods. Peak $\Delta CWTVD$ carries no such derivation. CWTVD has no likelihood for the peak to profile, so taking its maximum is the same scale-free summary applied by analogy, not an operation a nuisance-parameter argument singles out. Two things license the peak for CWTVD in place of that derivation, and they are distinct. The first is the resolving-power property of @sec-AC: that the peak gap between the two correlated geometries tracks the true mixture, so the maximised CWTVD gap carries the geometric signal the criterion is meant to read. This is a property of the mapping from mixture to gap and holds independent of sample size. The second is that the peak is an $\mathrm{argmax}$ over a curve realized at finite $N$, and a noisy curve can place its maximum where sampling alone opens a gap between geometries the truth does not separate. Resolving power does not speak to that: it says the gap responds to a real mixture imbalance, not that the $\mathrm{argmax}$ stays quiet under none. What certifies the finite-$N$ behaviour is the calibration of @sec-AE, which draws at the realized count and margins under a balanced truth and reads off how often the peak gap clears the threshold by noise alone. We run it where the concern is acute, the sparse high-OES Binary subset; in the well-populated subsets, which hold thousands of transitions, the argmax is stable for the same reason peak $\Delta KL$ is at those counts, and we do not extend the Binary calibration to them, since the noise depends on each subset's margins and not on its count alone. The justification for peaking CWTVD is thus empirical where the justification for peaking KL is analytic; we adopt the peak for both, holding them
co-equal, while noting the asymmetry in what each peak rests on.
 
The winner of the race is the cost matrix whose peak exceeds the nearest
rival's by at least 10\% on both criteria at once. There are two: a
likelihood criterion, peak $\Delta KL$, and a geometry-aware criterion,
peak $\Delta CWTVD$. The geometry-aware criterion is not a single score but
a one-parameter family, $\Delta CWTVD$ scored under the blend
$C_\lambda = \lambda C_{\text{skill}} + (1-\lambda) C_{\text{hierarchy}}$
for $\lambda \in [0,1]$; binary contributes no off-diagonal weight and so
drops out, leaving this segment as the whole space of geometry-aware
judges. We evaluate the family at its two endpoints, $C_{\text{skill}}$ and
$C_{\text{hierarchy}}$, because they are its most separated members: at a
fixed $\varepsilon$ the score is linear in $\lambda$, so the endpoints are
where a lead is hardest to hold across the family, but we adjudicate on the
peak over $\varepsilon$ and do not claim the fixed-$\varepsilon$
interpolation carries through the peak to certify the interior. The two
endpoints are therefore the two extreme informative judges, reported
jointly, not a proof of soundness at every interior blend. The two CWTVD
scorings are the two extremes of one criterion, not two independent
confirmations to be counted alongside $\Delta KL$: requiring a lead at
both is a joint condition on the one geometry-aware criterion, not a
second and third hurdle. A metric wins only if the likelihood endorses its
fit and the geometry-aware criterion endorses it at both endpoints, so a
plan that puts mass in roughly the right cells but at the wrong distances,
scoring high on $\Delta KL$ and low on either geometric endpoint, does not
win. Because the nearest rival can differ between the two judges, a winner
must lead whichever rival is closest under each.

Three outcomes follow, and
we report whichever obtains:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Decisive win.} One metric leads the nearest rival by 10\%
  at all three scoring points, peak $\Delta KL$ and peak $\Delta CWTVD$
  under each of the two informative judges, which between them instantiate
  the two criteria (the two CWTVD scores being the two endpoints of the one
  geometry-aware criterion). The race resolves in its favour.
  \item \textbf{Endpoint split.} The two geometric endpoints favour
  different metrics: one leads under $C_{\text{skill}}$-scoring, another
  under $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$-scoring. The winner is blend-dependent.
  Rather than a defect this is the design's most informative outcome, since
  a single blended judge would have crowned whichever metric led at the
  midpoint and concealed that the endpoints disagree. We report both, and
  the disagreement locates the mobility geometry of that regime as
  genuinely intermediate between the two rather than governed by either
  alone.
  \item \textbf{Unresolved.} No metric clears 10\% at all three scoring
  points and the two geometric endpoints do not cleanly favour different
  metrics.
  This covers both the case where the likelihood and geometry-aware
  criteria disagree about a single winner and the case where no candidate
  leads by 10\% on any criterion. We report which criteria favour which
  metric, since even an unresolved race describes how observed mobility
  departs from each candidate, but we name no governor.
\end{enumerate}
 
The 10\% threshold is an effect-size threshold, set in advance and applied
uniformly at all three scoring points. We treat two peak improvements differing
by less than ten percentage points as substantively equivalent regardless
of whether the difference is statistically distinguishable, on the grounds
that a smaller difference does not warrant naming one geometry the governor
of mobility in that regime. The threshold is substantive, not statistical, so
it does not flex with the number of scoring points: a gap below 10\% on a
geometric endpoint is substantively unimpressive whether it stands alone
or beside the others, and correcting the bar for the count of scores
would confuse a substantive effect-size threshold with a statistical
significance threshold. At the
sample sizes the linked census file provides, even the smallest sub-regime
holds thousands of transitions, so sampling noise in each peak gap is well
below this threshold and the binding constraint is the substantive one. The one
regime where this could fail is the high-OES Binary sub-regime, whose low
mobility leaves its off-diagonal cells sparse.

Once the transition data are available we run the following check. (see recipe) Take the high-OES Binary sub-regime's realized origin and destination margins, $a$ and $b$, and draw 1000 transition samples of size $N = \mathbf{1}^\top a$ from the entropic plan under a cost matrix that is a balanced mixture of the normalized skill and hierarchy geometries, $C = \tfrac{1}{2}(C_{\text{skill}}/7.145) + \tfrac{1}{2}(C_{\text{hierarchy}}/3)$, the two placed on a common scale by the fourth-percentile anchoring of @sec-cf. Each sample is scored with both geometric criteria exactly as the horse race does. This gives the distribution of the peak gap the criteria produce when the truth is a balanced mixture of the two geometries. Such a mixture is an intermediate cost structure that neither endpoint approximates, so neither should win decisively, and any gap on a given draw is manufactured by sampling noise at this regime's count. If fewer than 5% of draws produce a peak gap above 10%, a gap above 10% in the real data is informative and we read the Binary race normally. If balanced mixtures routinely clear 10%, the regime is noise-limited and we report it as such rather than reading its verdict.
 
An unresolved race is an informative no-decision rather than a coin to be
flipped. A disagreement between the likelihood-grounded and the
geometry-aware criteria, or between the two geometric endpoints, localizes
how a metric misfits, and breaking it by fiat would discard exactly the
signal the criteria were chosen to expose.

### Classifications and the lift adjustment

The horse race is run under two classifications of the same samples, the proxy classification of @sec-rp and the lift-adjusted (rescued) classification, and the lift adjustment behaves the same way wherever it is applied, so we state its logic once here as shared machinery before the global and sub-regime predictions draw on it.

The lift adjustment improves the fit of both skill and hierarchy on the local data and does not improve it on the non-local data. On the local side the adjustment removes leaked non-local transitions, the long credential-driven moves that the cost metrics assign low probability and whose presence degrades their fit, so their peak rises. On the non-local side the adjustment adds rescued wormholes and removes non-activating moves, if anything making the sample more movement-heavy, so skill and hierarchy fit it no better and may fit it worse. The prediction is therefore that the local-versus-non-local gap for these metrics widens under adjustment, strengthening the dissociation.

The lift adjustment does not help the binary metric on either sample. The transitions the adjustment moves between samples are off-diagonal moves, and binary does not model where movers go, so shuffling them changes neither its local nor its non-local fit. This is the control that makes the widening interpretable: the adjustment moves the structured metrics and leaves binary fixed, the same dissociation the global predictions below establish, seen a second time through the reclassification.

### The global local race {#sec-local-predictions}

The global local race pools all origin occupations and asks which single geometry best rationalizes the pooled local transitions, and, out of regime, whether that geometry fails on the non-local sample. It is the setup that motivates the partition rather than a result we defend: we do not believe a single geometry governs, and the pooled no-dominance we expect is what licenses cutting the sample into sub-regimes. This subsection is self-contained; the sub-regime grids of @sec-subregime-predictions build on the same machinery but run on a second axis this one does not have.

We commit in advance to two predictions, each following from the mechanism rather than fitted to the data, and separately state the motivating expectation the partition rests on.

First, the skill and hierarchy metrics fit the local sample, which carries no substantial increment proxy, better than the non-local sample, which carries a positive increment. The dissociation is a cross-sample comparison, so it is read on a single common measure, the neutral-blend $\Delta CWTVD$ against independence of @sec-local-falsification, rather than on the two-judge adjudication that decides the in-regime race: their peak on that measure sits above independence in the local sample and falls below it in the non-local sample. Local mobility is proximity-governed and these cost metrics predict short moves; non-local mobility is the credential-driven long jump they predict against.

Second, the binary metric does not show the systematic local-versus-non-local shift that skill and hierarchy do. Binary makes no off-diagonal bet, so its fit depends only on the aggregate stay/move split and not on where movers go, and it tunes $\varepsilon$ to each sample's move rate. Its peak fit is low in both samples, since it models none of the off-diagonal structure either sample carries; what matters for the dissociation is that it does not fall from the local to the non-local sample the way a metric that had made a geometric bet does, because binary made no bet to be caught out on. We therefore predict binary's peak fit is comparable across the two samples, not that it equals any particular level, and in any case does not participate in the directional collapse that identifies the structured metrics as regime-contingent.

The motivating expectation is that neither skill nor hierarchy is a clear winner on the pooled local data. Each governs its own sub-regime, so pooled across sub-regimes the two are close and neither clears the 10\% threshold. This no-dominance is not a prediction we defend on equal footing with the dissociation predictions above; it is the absence that motivates the partition, since a single global winner would itself count against the thesis that mobility is not one thing. The selection of @sec-rp bears on it in a specific direction: because it enriches the local sample with the short proximity-obeying moves that the graded metrics fit and binary cannot, it pushes the pooled race toward a spurious graded winner, against the no-dominance expectation rather than with it. A pooled result of no dominance is therefore conservative, having survived a selection that works to manufacture the global winner it denies. What we do if a clear winner appears despite this is set out in the contingency below, not treated as a refutation.

#### Out of regime: the non-local falsification {#sec-local-falsification}

The global race has a single out-of-regime axis, the non-local sample, where a new attainment has reset the worker's position. Because we expect no pooled winner, there is no single governing metric to carry out of regime; what the non-local runs establish is the dissociation itself. The graded metrics, which bet on where movers go, are predicted to fall below independence there, position having been reset; binary, which makes no such bet, is predicted to hold flat across the boundary, and that flatness is the control that marks the graded collapse as a geometric failure rather than non-local transitions being harder for every metric alike. The three metrics are therefore all scored on the non-local sample under both classifications. We state the below-independence method in full here; the sub-regime non-local leg of @sec-subregime-predictions refers back to it, where a per-regime governor does exist to be carried out of regime.

The falsification scores $\Delta CWTVD$ under a single neutral cost matrix
rather than under the two informative judges used to adjudicate the race.
That matrix is $C$, the arithmetic mean of the three normalized cost
matrices $C_{\text{skill}}$, $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$, and
$C_{\text{binary}}$, in which no candidate geometry is privileged. The race
needs two judges because it resolves a close comparative contest between
correlated geometries, and reading the verdict at both extreme informative
judges is what keeps a winner from being an artifact of one scoring choice. The falsification needs the opposite: not a comparison
but a single fixed line that a predicted metric either crosses or does not.
A neutral blend supplies exactly one such line, and scoring the crossing
under two judges instead would reintroduce the grey zone the fixed line is
meant to remove. This is the one role for which the blend, retired from
adjudication, remains the right instrument.

The out-of-regime criterion is stated against independence, on this
neutral geometry-aware measure. We state it for a single metric predicted
to govern, which is the sub-regime case; at the global level, where no one
metric governs, it applies to each graded metric in turn. In regime, the
metric predicted to govern
peaks above independence on $\Delta KL$ and on $\Delta CWTVD$ under the
neutral blend, since its geometry rationalizes the transitions and
improvement over independence is what the horse race measures. Out of
regime, where a new highest attainment resets the worker's position and
renders the 2016 occupation uninformative, that metric is predicted to
fall below independence on $\Delta CWTVD$.
 
The out-of-regime criterion rests on $\Delta CWTVD$ alone, and the reason
is that $\Delta KL$ cannot register the failure being tested. The
falsification asks whether the predicted metric has made the wrong
geometric bet, placing mass at the wrong distances. $\Delta CWTVD$ weights
each misallocation by distance and so penalises exactly this, falling below
independence when a short-move metric meets a movement-heavy matrix.
$\Delta KL$ is blind to geometry and scores any plan that captures the
diagonal stay/move structure, which every metric shares. A wrong-geometry
metric therefore collects partial KL credit for the diagonal even while its
off-diagonal bet is wrong, and its peak $\Delta KL$ can sit slightly above
independence rather than below it. This is visible in the simulations: in
the [online companion](https://rpmartin.github.io/not-one-thing-companion), under a binary data-generating process the skill and
hierarchy metrics peak below independence on $\Delta CWTVD$ but rise to a
small positive peak on $\Delta KL$ at moderate $\varepsilon$. Requiring the
geometry-blind measure to confirm a geometric failure would ask the wrong
instrument to register it. We therefore state the out-of-regime criterion
on $\Delta CWTVD$, the measure built to see what the falsification is about.
 
Setting the line at independence rather than at binary discharges the
conditionality that a binary benchmark would leave open. A wrongly
predicting metric always sits below binary out of regime, but whether its
$\Delta CWTVD$ also falls below independence depends on the non-local
transition matrix being movement-heavy: only when most credential-changers
move, and move far, does a short-move metric place enough mass on vacated
near pairs to fit worse than independence. We predict the non-local matrix
is movement-heavy, because the wormhole mechanism is precisely the claim
that a new credential drives long discontinuous jumps.

Because the crossing depends on that prediction holding, we separate it
from the verdict rather than fold it in. The non-local move rate is
directly observed, so we report it first, as a descriptive prior to any
$\Delta CWTVD$ score: whether the non-local matrix is movement-heavy is
settled by looking, not by the falsification. The below-independence test
is then read conditional on that first stage. If the matrix is
movement-heavy and the predicted metric crosses below independence, the
crossing confirms two things the mechanism asserts together, that the
metric made the wrong geometric bet out of regime and that the bet was
wrong because the jumps are long, and the falsification fires as designed.
If the matrix is movement-heavy and the metric nonetheless stays above
independence, the falsification fires against the design: the local
geometry is rationalizing transitions in a regime where a reset position
should have voided it, the outcome the double dissociation cannot survive.
If instead the first stage shows the matrix is not movement-heavy, the
below-independence test has no purchase to begin with, since a short-move
metric meeting a light matrix need not fit worse than independence; we
report the test as inapplicable rather than as either a pass or a design
failure, and the local model is neither falsified nor confirmed out of
regime by this route. Bundling the light-matrix case with the
governing-out-of-regime case would read a failed precondition as a
substantive failure, which the first stage exists to prevent.
 
Where the test applies, independence is a fixed point, so the crossing
itself is unambiguous. The predicted metric's $\Delta CWTVD$ peak is either
below zero or it is not, with no margin to calibrate and no grey zone to
adjudicate, where the race resolves a close contest between two correlated
geometries by asking whether one peak exceeds the other by 10\%. The two sides of the
falsification are also weaker bars than winning the race. A metric clears
the in-regime side by improving on independence at all, and fails the
out-of-regime side by crossing below it; the race is won only by leading
every rival by 10\% on both measures. Both skill and hierarchy peak well
above independence in either of their sub-regimes, since they are
correlated and each partially rationalizes the other's transitions, yet
only one wins. Improving on independence is necessary for a geometry to be
governing at all; leading by 10\% on both measures is what crowns it.
 
The mechanism that drives the predicted metric's $\Delta CWTVD$ below
independence is the same one that makes binary a useful point of
comparison. All three cost matrices assign zero self-distance,
$C_{ii} = 0$, so all three concentrate mass on the diagonal and capture the
dominant stay/move feature of the transition matrix. That diagonal
contribution is common to every plan, and what distinguishes the metrics is
the off-diagonal allocation. Binary makes no off-diagonal bet, since every
switch is equidistant under it, so it cannot be wrong about where movers
go. Skill and hierarchy do make that bet, and out of regime it is the wrong
one, because they place mass on geometrically proximate pairs that wormhole
movers avoid while the data concentrates on far pairs. A metric predicting
short moves into a movement-heavy matrix withholds mass from exactly where
the data sits, and $\Delta CWTVD$ penalises that misallocation by distance,
driving it below independence. The signature of this failure on
$\Delta CWTVD$ is a curve that rises monotonically toward the independence
baseline from below without crossing it, improving as $\varepsilon$ grows
only because diffusion toward independence is the one thing that helps a
metric whose geometry points the wrong way.
 

#### If a clear winner appears

The thesis rests on the sub-regime dissociation of @sec-subregime-predictions, not on the pooled race, so a clear global winner is not a refutation but a result to be read against the sub-regime grid, and we fix that reading in advance. If a metric wins the pooled race while the grid diagonal still holds, each metric governing its own subset, we reject the single-geometry claim and affirm regime-specific governance: the diagonal holding is the dissociation, so governance is regime-specific and the pooled winner is a compositional artifact of where movers concentrate across subsets, not evidence that one geometry governs. We report it as such, and the aggregate tilt toward the pooled winner is noted rather than read as global governance. If the diagonal collapses and the pooled winner is a graded metric, the thesis of regime-specific governance is falsified, and the pooled win does not establish global governance in its place: with the diagonal collapsed a pooled graded win is equally consistent with a compositional artifact, the selection above being one route to it, so we report it as classification- and selection-dependent rather than as global governance. The strongest form of this collapse is a single graded metric winning both the pooled race and every diagonal cell, the same geometry governing each sub-regime it was predicted to fail in; this is the one outcome that would affirmatively support single-geometry governance rather than merely fail to refute it, and we read it as such, against the thesis, subject to two conditions. The first is the selection caveat: the selection of @sec-rp works to manufacture a graded win, so a sweep is credited only because it survives that selection rather than being produced by it. The second is the global out-of-regime leg: a graded metric genuinely governing must fall below independence on the non-local sample once a new attainment resets the worker's position, while binary holds flat across that boundary, so we credit a graded sweep as global governance only when it is accompanied by this collapse across the local/non-local increment. A sweep that wins every diagonal cell but does not collapse out of regime is winning for some reason that survives the credential reset, which is not the geometry pricing proximity, and we do not read it as global governance. A graded sweep is therefore reported as evidence for global governance by that metric where a pooled graded win alone is not, the difference being that the sweep has won the sub-regime cells the compositional-artifact reading is built to explain, leaving no subset in which a rival geometry governs for composition to aggregate over. If the diagonal collapses and the winner is binary, geometry does not order destinations even within the sub-regimes designed to isolate where it should, and the finding is the negative one, that occupational distance does not organize local mobility in these data; we report it as such. Binary can also lead the pooled race while losing the graded subsets, if the movers concentrate in the segment binary governs, in which case the diagonal holds and the first reading applies. The one outcome the design cannot absorb is binary sweeping the diagonal, and because binary is scored as a genuine model throughout rather than as a straw man, that outcome would be a fair defeat of the geometric hypothesis rather than an artifact to explain away.

### The sub-regime grids {#sec-subregime-predictions}

The sub-regime analysis runs on two out-of-regime axes where the global race had one. The first is within the local sample, across the OES sub-regime boundaries: each metric is scored on each sub-regime subset, and a metric is predicted to fail away from its own. The second is across the local/non-local boundary, on the non-local transitions stripped by origin sub-regime: each sub-regime's hypothesised governor is scored on its own origin stripe, the graded governors predicted to fail there and binary predicted to persist. The two axes are distinct, the OES subset within local and the increment across the local/non-local boundary, and both bear on regime dependence. This subsection is self-contained on the first axis and refers back to @sec-local-predictions for the below-independence method the second axis shares.

#### Axis one: the off-diagonal grid

Within the local sample we score all three metrics on each of the three OES sub-regime subsets, the full three-by-three grid, and we do this under both the proxy and the lift-adjusted classifications, yielding two grids. We commit to the following.

First, on the diagonal each metric wins its own subset: skill in the Skill subset, hierarchy in the Hierarchy subset, binary in the Binary subset. Binary winning its own subset is a substantive result, the claim that where human capital is occupation-specific no distance geometry orders destinations, not a null.

Second, off the diagonal each metric fails away from its own subset. The winner tracking the diagonal as the subset changes is the within-local dissociation; a metric that led across the whole grid would show no regime dependence and would count against the thesis.

Third, the two grids exist to guard against a specific bias, not as a generic robustness check. Undetected leakage of non-local transitions into the local sample favours the binary metric, since a leaked wormhole is a long move that degrades skill and hierarchy while binary, making no off-diagonal bet, is unchanged (@sec-rp). Running both classifications is what makes this bias visible and correctable: the proxy grid carries the leakage, the lift-adjusted grid removes the part of it that leaves a lift signature, and the difference between the grids is the signature of the bias. That signature is committed in advance, skill and hierarchy rise and binary stays flat under adjustment, never the reverse; its location is not. A subset stable across the two grids is uncontaminated; a subset where the structured metrics rise is where leakage sorted. We do not presume leakage concentrates in any particular subset, since no origin-OES mechanism predicts that it should; we measure where it sorts.

Fourth, the adjustment corrects only the detectable leakage. The reclassification fires on a lift signature, so leaks that leave none, a credential that activated but carried the worker into an occupation it does not distinctively feed, remain in both grids. The proxy-versus-adjusted difference is therefore a lower bound on the total leakage, and the adjusted grid is de-contaminated but not clean. The residual signature-less leakage is handled not by the reclassification but by the residual-bias argument of @sec-rp, which shows it biases conservatively.

Fifth, we pre-commit to the reading of the Binary subset, where the favouring-binary bias would most damage a result we care about. If binary's win there narrows under adjustment but still clears the ten percent threshold, the win is robust against detectable leakage and against sparse-cell noise per @sec-AE, with the residual signature-less leakage arguing conservatively per @sec-rp rather than removed. If binary's win does not survive adjustment, the detectable leakage alone was enough to manufacture it, and we report the Binary subset's result as classification-dependent rather than claiming binary governs there. The don't-survive reading is decisive; the survive reading carries the residual caveat.

As a worker-level extension of the same logic, we pre-register a partition on age in place of OES, reported at access. The specificity OES reads at the level of the occupation has a counterpart in the individual career. Early on, when little occupation-specific capital has accumulated, the binding constraint on mobility is capability, and moves run along skill adjacency, near in skill space while dispersed across silos. By mid-career the worker has settled into a silo and moves within it, so the binding constraint is the silo boundary that hierarchical distance prices. Late in the career the reservation wage has risen far enough that few moves clear it and the survivors carry no systematic geometry, the condition the binary model describes. We cut the worker age distribution at 15 to 25, 25 to 40, and 40 and over, fixed in advance, and predict the winning metric shifts across these bands in the order skill, hierarchy, binary. The prediction is the order of the shift, not its sharpness. Age reaches the governing constraint only as a proxy for a proxy, the worker's clock for tenure and tenure for accumulated specific capital, and each band is internally heterogeneous in career stage, so we expect the partition to resolve mobility far less decisively than OES and margins within any band may be thin. A confirmation of the ordering through so degraded an instrument is independent corroboration of the specificity mechanism rather than a second decisive result; the disconfirming outcomes are a different order, no ordering, or a winner that does not move across the bands. The oldest band is populous in workers but sparse in moves, since the move rate falls with age, so we read its binary result only against the sparse-cell power check of @sec-AE, which establishes whether a graded signal of the size seen in the younger bands would have been detectable there had it been present.

One qualification to the nearest-rival rule is forced by the selection analysis of @sec-rp, and it is fixed here rather than chosen at access. In a sub-regime whose hypothesised governor is a graded metric, the selection into the local sample depresses binary's measured fit below what a preference-neutral sample would produce, so a graded metric's lead over binary is inflated by the selection rather than earned against it. We therefore do not count a graded metric's margin over binary toward its decisive-win condition in the Skill and Hierarchy sub-regimes: the graded governor must lead the other graded metric by 10\% at all three scoring points, and binary is set aside there as a downward-contaminated rival. The exclusion runs one way and only where the contamination does. It does not touch the Binary sub-regime, where binary is the hypothesised governor and the same selection runs against it, so its win over the graded metrics is earned against the grain of the bias and is scored against both (@sec-subregime-predictions). It does not touch the pooled global race, where binary's competitiveness is the phenomenon under test and its exclusion would delete the contest whose null result motivates the partition. The standard is mechanical, not discretionary: a rival is set aside only where its off-diagonal commitment leaves it exposed to the proximity mass the selection adds while the candidate's does not, which is the graded-over-binary case alone.

#### Axis two: the non-local grid, stripped by origin

The second grid tests each sub-regime's governor across the local/non-local boundary, on the non-local transitions stripped to that sub-regime's own origin occupations. A worker's 2016 occupation is observed even after a new attainment resets where their human capital is deployed, so the non-local sample splits by origin sub-regime, and a governor is tested only against the origins it was claimed to govern. The governor tested is the one the subset hypothesises in advance, not the one it realises, so the test is well defined even where the in-regime cell does not resolve; what such a case costs is interpretive, since the dissociation the test belongs to needs the in-regime leg to hold, not the running of the test itself.

The committed predictions sit on the diagonal and come in two kinds. For the graded sub-regimes the prediction is falsification, by the below-independence method of @sec-local-predictions: skill on the Skill-origin non-locals and hierarchy on the Hierarchy-origin non-locals are predicted to fall below independence, the credential reset having voided the origin their geometry priced. In regime each graded governor peaks above independence on both measures; out of regime its $\Delta CWTVD$ peak is predicted to fall below it.

For the Binary sub-regime the prediction is persistence, not falsification. Binary makes no distance bet in regime, so there is no geometric bet for the reset to break; but the Binary hypothesis is that these occupations defy distance-based rationalization, and that is a claim we hold rather than know, in regime and out alike. The out-of-regime form of it is invariance: we predict binary's fit on the Binary-origin non-locals resembles its fit on the Binary-origin locals, the sub-regime's defiance of distance surviving the one perturbation that resets everyone else. This is the sub-regime-localised counterpart of binary's role as the flat control in the global race, and it is corroboration by invariance rather than a below-independence crossing, since binary has no geometry to be caught pricing wrongly.

The Binary-origin non-local cell carries a second, independent prediction on the entry side, and it is a prediction about a rate, not about presence. The lock-in mechanism that defines the sub-regime predicts a low re-credentialing rate out of high-OES occupations, because workers already in a high-OES occupation rarely acquire a new highest attainment: occupation-specific human capital is reached through a single credentialing pipeline and confers no incentive to re-credential. Rarely is not never, so the mechanism predicts the cell is sparse, not empty, and a few workers in it are exactly what a low rate produces and confirm the premise rather than breaking it. The falsifying observation is accordingly a rate, not a body count: the cell falsifies lock-in only if workers leave Binary-origin occupations to re-credential at a rate comparable to the rate out of the Skill and Hierarchy origins, so the test is the Binary-origin re-credentialing rate against those graded-origin baselines, with the Binary-origin stock as the denominator, and a single worker or a handful reads as confirmation of near-emptiness. This entry-side rate prediction and the persistence prediction the populated part of the cell carries pull in opposite directions on the same cell, and the reconciliation is that they speak to different quantities: lock-in wants a low rate relative to the graded origins, while persistence wants enough absolute moves to score the horse race, and a small count can be both a low rate against a large Binary-origin stock and enough moves to fit a race. Where the cell is too sparse even for that, the persistence leg is reported as underpowered rather than run, per @sec-AE, while the rate reading stands on its own. The remaining out-of-regime content of the Binary hypothesis lies further on the entry side and is carried by the EOS--OES association of the non-local model rather than by a horse race.

The off-diagonal cells of this grid carry no committed prediction. We score them so that a subset whose realised winner is not its hypothesised governor can still be read out of regime: if skill unexpectedly leads the Hierarchy locals, its behaviour on the Hierarchy-origin non-locals is then available as reported exploration rather than a post-hoc scramble. Scoring the full grid on both axes, within-local and origin-stripped non-local, is what keeps every result, expected or surprising, legible out of regime.

## Non-Local Model {#sec-non_local}

The non-local regime is where the horse race predicts occupational geometry to fail: once a new attainment resets the worker's position, distance in skill or hierarchy space no longer orders where they go, and the geometric metrics collapse toward independence. That failure is a negative result on its own, a regime the geometry does not govern, and it leaves a question the horse race cannot answer, what governs there instead. This section is the paper's positive account of that regime, and the reason to care about the relationship it tests is that account rather than the relationship taken by itself.

The stakes are threefold. First, the paper's thesis is that mobility is not one thing, and a dissociation is far stronger with both arms than with one: the horse race supplies the negative arm, that no single geometry governs non-local moves, and an EOS--OES linkage supplies the positive arm, that credential specificity orders those moves where distance does not. Without it the non-local regime is a hole in the geometry; with it the regime is governed by a second organizing principle orthogonal to the first, and *not one thing* becomes the presence of two structures rather than the absence of one. Second, the linkage is policy-actionable in a way distance is not: occupations cannot be moved closer in skill space, but credentials can be made more or less specific, and if specificity-matching governs the non-local regime then the design of credentials is a lever on where retrained workers land and how tightly they are channelled there, which speaks directly to apprenticeship and credentialing policy. Third, the strength of the relationship is itself the quantity of interest, a weak linkage meaning credentials are loose signposts and a strong one meaning they are rails.

All three stakes depend on the relationship carrying information beyond a tautology. That specific credentials pair with specific occupations is nearly true by construction, since a credential is defined by the occupation it gates; the finding earns its stakes only if it says more than that credentialed workers hold the jobs their credentials are for. The gap and collapse below are what supply the more: they establish that the linkage is forward-directed and triggered by acquisition rather than a standing feature of who holds what, and it is that forward, credential-triggered content, not the bare pairing, that the three stakes rest on. Should the gap come in near zero, the relationship reduces to the tautology, the non-local regime has no positive account, and the honest reading is that it is governed by nothing the design can name, a null that is informative for the thesis but a materially weaker and different result.

The non-local model asks whether the specificity of a worker's newly acquired education and the specificity of the occupation they reach are linked at the individual level. It is built from the two marginal specificities defined at @sec-rp, OES on the occupation side and EOS on the education side, read off the public education$\times$NOC table, together with a pairing that only the linked file supplies.

Each marginal is defensible on its own and neither is derivable from the other. What the public table cannot establish is that they are connected: that the high-EOS educations and the high-OES occupations are the same specificity showing up at the two ends of a worker's history, the education acquired and the occupation later held. The top of the EOS ranking and the top of the OES ranking contain fields and occupations whose names echo one another, but a cross-section is a standing stock, not a record of sequence, and co-occurrence in a snapshot cannot distinguish an education acquired before the occupation was reached from two independently specific margins that happen to share a vocabulary. Establishing the link requires observing the same worker acquire the education and then arrive at the occupation, which is what the linked file provides and the public table cannot.

For each credential-acquirer we attach the EOS of the education acquired within the window and the OES of both their 2016 and 2021 occupations, and ask first whether the acquired education's EOS co-varies with the destination occupation's OES across workers. The prediction is a positive individual-level association: workers who acquire highly specific educations arrive in highly specific occupations. We make no causal claim. The association is a pattern, that the two specificities travel together through realized transitions, and the mechanism we offer for it, occupation-specific human capital opening a path to the occupation that uses it, is an interpretation of the pattern rather than something the estimate identifies.

Because EOS is a property of the education and OES a property of the occupation, every worker sharing an education carries the identical EOS and every worker sharing an occupation the identical OES, so the individual-level association is a pattern over education--occupation pairings weighted by how many workers traverse each. We estimate it as the slope of a standardized regression, which recovers the correlation, and cluster standard errors three ways, on education, on occupation, and on worker, to respect that dependence: education and occupation carry the shared-value dependence just described, while worker enters because the stacked origin--destination specification of @sec-non_local-predictions contributes two rows per worker, and the two share the same person. The estimator we read from this clustering is selected by the effective cluster counts at access, the analytic three-way variance where the counts permit and a permutation test where they do not, as set out in @sec-non_local-inference.

**The gap.** A positive EOS--OES association on its own is weak evidence, because a latent disposition toward specificity, a worker drawn to specific credentials who also sorts into specific occupations for reasons unrelated to any path between them, would produce it. We separate the mechanism from that disposition with a within-worker contrast: we estimate the acquired education's EOS association with the destination occupation's OES and with the origin occupation's OES, and compare them. The mechanism predicts the association is stronger for the destination than for the origin, and the gap between the two is what the newly acquired credential adds.

The gap is robust to the latent-disposition confound for a reason of timing. A time-invariant disposition toward specificity loads on origin and destination alike, since it is a fixed trait of the worker present at both the origin and destination occupations, so it raises both associations together and differences out of the gap. The newly acquired credential cannot load on the origin, because the origin predates it: the credential did not exist, operatively, when the worker occupied the 2016 occupation, so whatever forward reach it has toward the destination it cannot have toward the origin. The gap therefore isolates the credential's forward reach from any fixed specificity the worker carried into the transition.

One form of the disposition is not time-invariant and so is not differenced out by this argument: a disposition that drifts forward over a career, creeping up the specificity ladder through ordinary opportunity rather than through any credential. Such a drift separates origin from destination in the same direction the credential does, because both are functions of elapsed time within the window, so timing alone cannot tell a forward-reaching trait from a forward-reaching credential. What separates them is the cross-sample falsification of @sec-non_local-predictions. A credential-independent drift operates whether or not a credential is acquired, so it should raise the destination association above the origin association among local movers too, where no credential was acquired within the window. The mechanism predicts the forward gap collapses there; a forward drift predicts it persists. The local-mover check therefore discriminates the two: a collapse rules out a drift that operates alike whether or not a credential is acquired, and what remains is a drift concentrated in the credential-acquirers themselves, either switched on by the credential, which is not an alternative to the mechanism but the mechanism itself, or running faster in the workers who retrain, which is the asymmetric-forward disposition set aside among the identifying assumptions as the one the design does not discharge. The only confounder the gap does not remove is thus the same one it never claimed to, a trait that links the acquired credential specifically to the destination and not the origin, which is the mechanism the design describes rather than an alternative to it.

We estimate the gap in a single model, stacking each worker's origin and destination OES into one outcome column with a role indicator and interacting EOS with role; the interaction coefficient is the gap, and its standard error, clustered on education, occupation, and worker, is the inference. The companion display is a two-panel traffic-weighted scatter, destination OES against EOS beside origin OES against EOS, in which the gap is the difference in slope between the panels.

#### Inference {#sec-non_local-inference}

The association is estimated over individuals, but EOS is a property of the education and OES of the occupation, so all workers sharing an education carry the identical EOS and all sharing an occupation the identical OES. Treating workers as independent would badly overstate precision. We keep the worker as the unit of observation, which fixes the point estimate at the traffic-weighted pattern, and place the dependence in the variance estimator; aggregating to education--occupation pairings first would not help, since pairings still share educations and occupations and would themselves require the same clustering. The variance is clustered three ways. Education and occupation carry the shared-value dependence just described; worker enters as a third margin because the stacked origin--destination specification contributes two rows per worker, sharing the same person, so the worker margin is required for correctness even though it is not a fragile one, its clusters being uniformly of size two and hence numerous and balanced. An occupation forms a single cluster spanning every row in which it appears, whether as a worker's origin or another's destination: the shared OES value it induces is the same number regardless of role, so the residual correlation it carries spans both roles, and splitting the origin and destination appearances of one occupation into separate clusters would miss exactly that cross-role dependence. The occupation cluster is therefore the occupation, not the occupation-by-role.

The point estimate is well powered but the inference is not automatically so, and the two turn on different quantities. Every variable the non-local model requires, occupation in both cycles, field of education, and work activity, is long-form only, the short form being a demographic head count that carries none of them, so the estimand lives on the intersection of the two 25\% long-form samples, on the order of a sixteenth of the population. In worker terms this is still a large sample, hundreds of thousands of usable transitions even after the credential-acquisition condition and the observed-occupation requirement, so the point estimates are well powered; scarcity of workers is not the concern. The concern is the cluster count, a different and far smaller quantity: inference runs on the number of distinct educations and occupations, not the number of workers, since everyone sharing an education carries the identical EOS and their residuals are correlated. A margin can hold hundreds of thousands of workers across a few hundred clusters. Cluster-robust asymptotics depend on the effective number of clusters, well approximated by the inverse-Herfindahl count $(\sum_g n_g)^2 / \sum_g n_g^2$ over cluster sizes $n_g$, rather than on the nominal number of educations or occupations; a skewed size distribution that concentrates workers in a few large clusters drives the effective count far below the nominal one, and on a populated but concentrated margin it can land in genuinely few-clusters territory rather than merely below its nominal value.

Which of education and occupation is the more fragile margin is not settled by the construction, and we do not claim to predict it. What the sampling does support is a one-sided claim about occupation. The sample conditions on credential acquisition, and among acquirers are a set of very high-traffic generic fields, the bachelor's degrees in arts, commerce, and general science that dominate credential flows. These fields fan out across the labour market, dispersing their holders over many destination occupations, so the occupation margin receives workers from many educations and no single occupation swallows a dominant share. That dispersion is what supports the occupation margin's effective cluster count: the fanning-out educations spread destination mass widely, which is the condition a healthy occupation margin needs. The education margin is a different matter and we leave it open. It is a mixture, the same high-traffic generic fields alongside a tail of specific credentials that funnel narrowly, and whether its effective count clears the few-clusters range depends on the whole size distribution across educations, which the fan-out argument does not characterize. The presence of a few large generic fields does not by itself settle the education count, since a populous spread of mid-sized educations can carry it even when a handful of fields are large. We therefore expect occupation to be well-populated in effective terms and make no matching prediction for education.

This occupation claim is worth pressing on directly, since it is the one the regime choice can lean on. For occupation to concentrate despite the fan-out, the large generic credentials would have to feed a small common set of high-inflow catch-all destinations, general managers, administrative officers, retail supervisors, piling occupation-margin mass onto a few large clusters. This is not impossible, since fan-out requires destinations to be numerous but not that inflows be even, and generic credentials do feed catch-all occupations disproportionately. But it requires destinations to be many yet lopsided; the alternative, a single credential feeding a single occupation, concentrates occupation only in the specific-credential profile that is by construction the low-traffic tail and cannot dominate the margin. High traffic and tight destination concentration are close to mutually exclusive in this sample, which is why we expect occupation to clear the few-clusters range. Nothing beyond that rides on it: both effective counts are computed at access and the regime is chosen by them, so the fan-out argument supplies only a reason to expect enough effective occupation clusters, and the permutation fallback covers whatever the education count turns out to be.

We do not rest on the prior, since the effective counts are unknown before access, and we commit to the full decision rule now. We report the effective cluster count, by the inverse-Herfindahl measure above, for education, occupation, and worker at access, and the estimator we read is selected by those counts before the gap is seen. Where all three effective counts clear the few-clusters range, primary inference is the analytic three-way cluster-robust variance, which handles all three margins at once and delivers a confidence interval on the gap, the quantity the section is built to read. Where any margin's effective count falls into few-clusters territory, the analytic variance is untrustworthy on that margin, and no one-margin resampling repairs it cleanly: a wild cluster bootstrap resampling the fragile margin corrects that margin only by ceasing to cluster the others, trading a broken leg for a dropped one rather than fixing the estimator, and there is no cleanly specified multiway wild cluster bootstrap that resamples the fragile margin while still clustering the rest. We therefore do not use the bootstrap. Primary inference in the fragile regime is instead a permutation test on the EOS--role interaction. Holding OES, occupation, role, and the within-worker pairing fixed, we permute the acquired-education labels across workers, both of a worker's stacked rows carrying the same reassigned EOS, and rebuild the null distribution of the gap directly. This handles the two dependences in a single operation and for a single reason: permuting education labels as whole-worker blocks preserves the education tie structure exactly, so the test never invokes a large-cluster asymptotic on education and its validity is indifferent to how few effective education clusters there are; and because occupation, OES, and role are never disturbed, the occupation dependence is carried into every permuted dataset identically to the real data rather than dropped, so it too is handled without an asymptotic. The permutation test rests on exchangeability of EOS across workers under the null, which is the same maintained identifying assumption the design carries elsewhere, the asymmetric-forward disposition of the identifying-assumptions section, and not a new or weaker one; it fixes the inference problem the cluster counts pose without touching identification. What it delivers is a valid $p$-value for the null of no forward gap rather than an interval on the gap's magnitude: we accept that trade, reading significance rather than a trustworthy interval in the fragile regime, while the point estimate, which is well powered regardless of cluster counts, still carries the magnitude. One limit on the fallback is worth stating in advance: if the education margin is concentrated, the number of distinct whole-worker relabelings is limited, and the achievable $p$-value granularity is bounded by that concentration, so in a highly concentrated case the permutation floor is coarser than a continuous $p$-value; we report the realized granularity at access rather than presume it fine. We report which regime obtained and which estimator it selected, rather than choosing after seeing the gap.

To keep each cluster non-degenerate and to bound the leverage of thinly-acquired cells, the association is estimated over educations acquired by at least ten workers in the non-local sample and, symmetrically, over occupations reached by at least ten, a cluster-floor of ten set in advance and applied to both clustering margins at access. Ten is a convention rather than a theorem: it clears with margin the range below which a cluster contributes negligible independent information and singleton and doubleton clusters destabilize the cluster-robust variance, and it is round enough to carry no hidden researcher degree of freedom. What makes it defensible here is that it is fixed before access on a data-independent rationale, not that any external standard blesses the number; it is an analytic choice about what enters the estimation, distinct from and prior to any decision about what output may be released. The cluster-floor applies symmetrically because the floor guards against a different failure than concentration and either margin can suffer it: singleton and doubleton clusters destabilize the cluster-robust variance on whichever margin they fall, and neither margin is exempt from a thin tail, education from rarely-acquired credentials and occupation from rarely-reached destinations, so protecting cluster count on only one would leave the other exposed. The same cluster-floor incidentally removes the rarest and most misreport-prone credentials, attenuating the masking discussed in @sec-non_local-limits. The magnitude of the association is the substantive quantity: where cluster counts permit we report it with a cluster-robust interval, and where they do not we report the point estimate with a permutation test of the null, reading significance there rather than a trustworthy interval.


### Predictions and out-of-regime falsification {#sec-non_local-predictions}

We commit in advance to three predictions, following from the mechanism of @sec-non_local rather than fitted to the data, together with a validation check on the first. The first is a baseline the other two are read against, and the second and third are falsifications, one within the non-local sample and one against the local sample; both falsifications turn on the timing logic already given, that a freshly acquired credential postdates the 2016 occupation and so can reach forward to the destination but not back to the origin. The identifying content is in the second and third, not the first: the baseline association is confounded on its own, and it is the gap and the collapse that separate the mechanism from a standing specificity disposition, down to the single asymmetric-forward residual named in @sec-non_local as the one the design does not discharge.

First, on the non-local sample, the EOS of the acquired education is positively associated with the OES of the destination occupation. This is the baseline, not yet a finding: on its own it is consistent with the pipeline mechanism and equally with a standing disposition toward specificity that sorts a worker into specific credentials and specific occupations alike, and it does not discriminate the two. Its role is to establish the existence, level, and sign of the linkage that the gap then differences and the local-sample collapse falsifies against; a within-worker forward gap is uninterpretable without the baseline association it is a contrast within. What identifies the mechanism is the conjunction of this baseline with the two predictions below, not the baseline itself.

Second, on the non-local sample, the destination association exceeds the origin association: the EOS--OES gap is positive. This is the within-sample falsification. A gap of zero would say the acquired education is no more tied to where the worker went than to where they started, which is what a standing disposition toward specificity, linking both occupations alike, would produce; a positive gap is the signature of the credential doing the placing, and it is what marks the pattern as credential-driven rather than a trait of the worker.

Third, on the local sample restricted to workers who moved, the gap collapses. Absent a new credential the worker's education is stale, operative already in 2016 and unchanged through 2021, a standing attribute carried through the move rather than a force that produced it, so it links to origin and destination at similar strength and shows no forward advantage. This is the cross-sample falsification, and it uses the local movers. The contrast between the two samples is not between movement and stasis, since both are conditioned on movement, but between a credential acquired within the window and one predating it: the forward gap is present when the credential is new enough to have done the placing and absent when it is not. We commit to the collapse; a stale credential that showed the same forward reach as a fresh one would falsify the timing account on which the mechanism rests. The collapse also carries the weight of separating the mechanism from a forward-drifting disposition: such a drift is credential-independent and would raise the destination association above the origin one among these credential-less movers, so its absence here is what rules it out where the differencing of @sec-non_local could not. A gap that instead leaned backward, the stale education linking more strongly to origin than destination, would corroborate the account further, but we do not commit to it, and the committed prediction is the collapse of the forward advantage rather than its reversal.

A validation accompanies the demonstration. The association of the first prediction is between two marginals, the education's EOS and the occupation's OES, and a marginal association cannot by itself distinguish matching from coincidence: a high-EOS credential whose holder lands in an unrelated high-OES occupation, an optometry graduate who somehow becomes a dentist, contributes to the association exactly as a genuine pipeline does, though the credential does not feed that occupation at all. What separates the two is the lift of the worker's realized education--destination cell, $m(e, n_{2021})$, the one quantity that reads the pairing rather than either margin. We commit in advance to the association being concentrated in high-lift realized transitions: restricted to movers whose acquired credential distinctively feeds their destination, the association is present, and among movers whose realized cell is at or below baseline lift, a specific credential landing where it has no pipeline, it is not. It is the contrast between the two subsets that certifies matching, not the vanishing in the low-lift subset alone: the association's survival among the genuine pipelines rules out that its absence among the coincidental pairings is merely the lower power of a smaller or noisier subset. Were the association instead indifferent to realized lift, the two specificities would be co-occurring in workers without the channel that connects them, and the matching interpretation would fail. At access we also report the high-EOS, high-OES pairings by traffic with their lift, a legible catalogue in which the genuine pipelines appear at high lift and the coincidental pairings, if the interpretation is right, do not appear at all.

Two features of the samples bear on the cross-sample falsification, and both make it conservative. First, a subtle contamination runs the other way: a credential-gated move whose increment went unrecorded, the nurse-aide to licensed-practical-nurse case of @sec-cf, is routed local by the proxy classification though the mechanism would call it non-local. Such a leaked worker carries genuine forward reach into the local sample, which works against the predicted collapse rather than manufacturing it, since a leaked wormhole can only lift the local forward gap toward the non-local value and narrow the contrast. The lift-based reclassification of @sec-rp recovers these workers, and the proxy-versus-rescued contrast measures how much leakage there was; the collapse is predicted under both classifications and more sharply under the rescued one. Second, the credential-less mover sample is not thin but large: credential acquisition within a five-year window is rare, so non-acquirers vastly outnumber acquirers and the local-mover falsification runs on the populous side of that split. The falsification is therefore well powered to detect a credential-independent forward drift if one exists, and a collapse is strong confirmation rather than a failure-to-detect on a thin sample. What survives the falsification does so for a structural reason, not a power one: a forward-reaching disposition that is coextensive with credential acquisition, present only in the workers who retrain, is absent from the credential-less sample by construction, so no sample size can detect it there. The large sample decisively removes every credential-independent alternative and leaves exactly the credential-bundled residual, which is unfalsifiable by this route in principle rather than merely unmeasured, the asymmetric-forward disposition named in @sec-non_local as indistinguishable from the wormhole by construction. We report the local falsification at access with its realized size, but its force rests on the structural argument, not on clearing a power bar the large sample clears easily.

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

### Local Mobility

Two sample restriction mechanisms introduce a potential selection
concern for local mobility. Non-linkage and non-observability of
occupation are both disproportionately concentrated among
low-attachment workers, individuals with casual, seasonal, or
intermittent employment whose identifying information is also less
stable across census cycles, so the two filters largely co-select
the same low-skill population rather than introducing independent
exclusions. This shared exclusion is not neutral in occupational
space: it concentrates in the low-OES, low-skill region and removes
disproportionately short-range transitions, the adjacent low-skill
moves that casual employment generates. Its first-order effect is on
the representativeness of population-level transition estimates
(external validity).

Whether it also threatens the internal validity of the horse race
turns on a narrower condition than the occupational concentration
itself. The horse race is a relative comparison, so removing a region
of occupational space does not bias the adjudication between metrics
unless, within that region, the excluded transitions are
differentially rationalizable by one metric than the retained ones.
Concentration alone is insufficient: if excluded moves are easier for
every metric to fit, because they are short and short moves are easy
for any cost structure, all three metrics' fits fall together and the
ranking is undisturbed. The bias requires the excluded moves to be
easier for one particular metric, and the natural candidate is the
skill metric, since a casual worker taking the nearest available job
produces exactly the short-in-skill-space transition the skill metric
rewards. The live threat is therefore specific: excluding
low-attachment workers may deflate the skill metric's measured fit
relative to hierarchy and binary, biasing the race against skill.

This threat cannot be tested directly, because the excluded
transitions are by construction not in the sample: an unlinked or
occupation-missing worker has no origin--destination pair to score
against any cost matrix. Two indirect handles bound it instead, each
testing sensitivity along an observable attachment gradient and
extrapolating to the unobserved. First, labour-market attachment is
itself partially observable on the in-sample workers through the
census work-activity classification, which orders individuals by weeks
worked and full- versus part-time intensity over the reference year.
We re-estimate the local race on the low-attachment and high-attachment
strata and report whether the metric ranking, and the skill metric's
fit in particular, moves between them; a skill tilt among observed
casual workers is the best available evidence for the sign of the bias
from excluding the unobserved ones. Three caveats bound this handle.
The work-activity reference year is the calendar year before each
census, so the 2021 measure falls in 2020 and is contaminated by
pandemic labour disruption, for which reason we prefer the 2016 (2015
reference) measure where both are available. Work activity is a
long-form (25\% sample) variable, which is no additional restriction
here, since the linked frame is already the intersection of the two
long-form samples. The stratum that bears on the threat is unlikely to
be the scarce one: low-attachment workers are a large share of the
labour force, and the sample is conditioned on occupational
transitions, which low-attachment workers make more often than
stably-employed ones, so mobility conditioning tends to over-represent
rather than deplete them, and the low-OES region they occupy is where
transitions concentrate rather than thin out. We therefore expect the
low-attachment stratum to be adequately populated for the stratified
race, but do not rely on it: the realized cell counts in that stratum
are not known until access, and where they turn out too sparse to
detect a skill tilt of the magnitude at issue, the stratified race is
reported as underpowered rather than as evidence of no tilt, per the
detection-power logic of @sec-AE. Absence of a detectable tilt in a
stratum too small to detect one is not evidence the tilt is absent.
Second, where the linkage is probabilistic and carries a match score,
we sweep the linkage threshold and re-run the race across progressively
looser link sets, which admit disproportionately the marginally-linked,
identifier-unstable workers; a ranking stable across the sweep is
evidence the contest is insensitive to link quality, the
identifier-stability correlate of attachment.

Neither handle is a direct test, and their force rests on a
monotonicity assumption we state rather than verify: that the
unlinkable and occupation-missing workers lie further along the same
attachment gradient as the marginally-linked and observed-casual
populations, resembling more of the same rather than a qualitatively
different group. This is an identifying assumption of the same kind as
the asymmetric-forward disposition named for the non-local gap, one the
design bounds but does not discharge, and we report the two
sensitivities as evidence for it rather than as proof that the
exclusion is innocuous.

A notable omitted factor for local mobility  is \emph{path-specific} wage differentials. The additively separable component of wage gains, recoverable from origin and destination wage levels alone, is absorbed by the 
margins insofar as high-wage destinations attract larger inflows and 
low-wage origins larger outflows. The residual dyadic component, 
reflecting transition-specific wage premia and discounts beyond what 
origin and destination wage levels predict, is an omitted factor. 
Short-distance transitions are within a similar occupational 
neighbourhood, reducing employer uncertainty about candidate fit and 
productivity; long-distance transitions cross larger skill or 
hierarchical gaps, and employers may discount wage offers to 
compensate for that uncertainty, or workers may accept lower wages 
to gain entry to a distant occupation.

Thus, path-specific wage differentials are better understood as an 
alternative mechanism, rather than a confounder. If employers use the same metric that governs mobility to assess candidate fit uncertainty, discounting wages for transitions that are long under the winning metric, that discount reinforces worker selection toward shorter transitions under 
the same metric. Both channels predict identical patterns of 
transitions and are equally consistent with the winning metric being 
the correct description of the mobility geometry. The horse race 
identifies which distance geometry best rationalizes observed 
transitions in a reduced-form sense, but cannot separately attribute 
that rationalization to worker or employer preferences regarding 
distance.

### Non-Local Mobility {#sec-non_local-limits}

The non-local design faces limitations of four kinds, taken here in turn: a scope restriction on which moves the estimand covers, two measurement threats that bias the association downward, an inferential limitation from the small number of clusters the standard errors rest on, and a limit on what the gap identifies, which is a directional pattern rather than causation.

The non-local regime studies non-negative operative increments, as defined in @sec-rp: transitions where the operative credential rises above the worker's prior ceiling or respecifies at the same level. Substitutive moves, where an over-credentialed worker retrains below their ceiling and repositions on a sub-maximal credential, lie outside the estimand and are invisible to a highest-attainment record; the findings therefore speak to additive and lateral specific-human-capital activation, not to occupational mobility of every kind. This is a scope of the question rather than a gap in the answer, and it is consistent with the paper's premise that mobility is not one thing: the substitutive channel is a distinct phenomenon with its own economics, deserving its own treatment rather than absorption into this one.

The non-local partition is restricted to individuals who acquire a new highest educational attainment between 2016 and 2021 and report an occupation in both periods. A 2016 occupation is observed if and only if the individual was employed between May 1st and 7th, the 2016 census reference week. For the 2015/2016 school year, roughly half of 18-29 year old students reported concurrent work, with an (unweighted) ten percentage point decrease for university students, consistent with more intensive programs suppressing concurrent employment.^[source: Statistics Canada table 37-10-0104-01.] The Census reference week provides a partial offset: falling after the typical post-secondary academic year ends, it captures individuals who have recently finished exams and may have already begun summer employment. But this offset is weaker for intensive professional programs that are either year-round or have students for whom summer employment is atypical. The resulting truncation is not random: missingness is concentrated among the most occupationally specific educations, the high-EOS credentials that anchor the strongest pipelines, where the association the model predicts is sharpest. A worker missing a 2016 occupation is dropped, so these are disproportionately the specific-credential acquirers whose destination the mechanism most cleanly predicts, and their absence weakens the measured EOS--OES association rather than strengthening it, so the estimate is a lower bound. Notably, this missingness pattern is not purely a limitation: the disproportionate absence of 2016 occupations among the most specific credentials is itself consistent with the wormhole mechanism, since program intensity and specificity are precisely what suppresses concurrent employment. In the online companion we plot each education's occupational specificity against the share of its workers missing a 2016 occupation, quantifying the magnitude of this truncation.

```{r}

# #| tbl-cap: "Share of students employed during program, by age and institution type"

#           type_of_institution_attended %in% c("College","University"),

#

#      linesep = ""

#    general_title = "Source:",

#    escape = FALSE
```
